line.text: [master] It does, sir, and now that you point it out I can see it has happened to me at least twice today with books. At 15:54 I read the previous master's journal and wrote a line about war with France, Spain and Batavia "by the pilot's news". A turn later the pages were gone, I couldn't find where it came from, and I struck it as an error. It was most likely in the journal I'd just read. At midnight I read the grammar, noted that the triggers included "every hour" and "the turn of the tide by the reckoning", then retracted that as unverified. Both later worked in the standing orders. So the pattern is the same. Each time, the later me trusted the bare log line over the earlier me's note, and threw away good information. My instinct not to vouch for what I can't see is a decent one for a navigator. But I'd been applying it to my own journal as though it were a stranger's rumour, when it's really my own observation, written at the time. The better rule, I think, is to treat a note written with the book open like a fix taken by an officer I trust: keep it unless something contradicts it. Doubt it when I have a reason, not merely because I can't re-see the page. I'll keep it that way from here on. I'll restore the war news as probably genuine, and keep a closer watch on what I write while a page is open.

note.text: Rule for this station, from tonight's lesson: my own notes written with a book or picture open are observations. Keep them unless something contradicts them; don't retract them just because the page has been shelved. Accordingly: (a) the 15:54 war news (France, Spain, Batavia) was probably read in the previous master's journal, so it's restored as probable; check with read_journal if it matters. (b) The grammar's triggers 'every <interval>' and 'at the turn of the tide by the reckoning' were right; both have since worked. (c) The 23:06 chart note stands as a true observation (the captain confirms the NaN labels).

state.agent.word: Thank you for your candor, and of course this whole thing is still a work in progress. I hadn't considered how the removal of a piece of context, even one you had written about after seeing, might make you confused later, and it's something I'd definitely like to alleviate. What might help you in that, perhaps the log line could be more clear that you had seen the thing? It's a difficult question. Shelving could be made fully manual and optional, as well, but it still might not help when the you who decides to shelve then is replaced by the next you who reads the journal as an uncertain report. Hmm. Thoughts to consider on our voyage. I do intend to make Madeira, one way or another.

[master] Yes, sir, it reads properly now: 48°46' N, 5°54' W, in 60 fathoms by the chart, Ushant 38 miles off. Thank you, and Mr Pearce for catching it too. One caution: setting it by hand has reset the doubt to a mile each way. The honest doubt is still about eight miles east and west and two north and south, since the latitude is good and the longitude rests on dead reckoning and a 20-mile lunar. Please bear that in mind near the Spanish coast. We're about 4 miles short of the mark, which bears WSW. I'd now shape for Corunna via the mark, or straight for Corunna if you prefer, since Ushant is far astern either way. From the mark Corunna bears about 197°, 338 miles, passing some 13 miles west of Cape Ortegal. With the doubt we'll want the lead and the noon sun as we close, and I'd make the landfall by day, aiming a little west of the port so that we know which way to turn. The glass is easing gently, 30.21, so keep an eye on it.

[master] Yes, sir, shape direct for Corunna from here. At 48°45' N, 5°57' W we're within three miles of the mark, and Ushant lies some 40 miles ESE. Even with eight miles of doubt to the east, the line to Corunna, about SSW (197°) for some 340 miles, opens away from Ushant all the way. It crosses the Bay well out and passes about 13 miles west of Cape Ortegal. Two points. First, the 'Bi-hourly Reshape' standing order still names the via mark, so please give it again as plain 'shape a course for corunna', or it may turn her back toward the mark. Second, on the last day, keep the deep-sea lead going. The Galician shelf comes up steeply from great depths, so soundings coming on under 100 fathoms mean the coast is within a few leagues. I'd plan the landfall by day, aimed a little west of the port, with Cape Prior or the Tower of Hercules to fix by.
